questions.q: What two things make up the liqueur d'expédition added at dosage?
accept: wine and rectified concentrated grape must
questions.exp: The liqueur d'expédition is wine with sugar dissolved in it, traditionally cane sugar, though many houses now use concentrated grape must; how much goes in sets the style from Extra Brut to Doux. Brut Nature takes no added sugar at all, and the Court asks what both liqueurs are made of.

questions.q: Which pair does the liqueur de tirage add to the still base wine to start the second fermentation?
questions.exp: The liqueur de tirage is sugar and selected yeast, with a riddling aid such as bentonite, stirred into the still cuvée at bottling; the yeast ferments the sugar in the bottle and the carbon dioxide stays dissolved. About 24 grams of sugar per litre gives a pressure of around six atmospheres.

questions.q: Which country's traditional method sparkling wine carries the name Cap Classique?
questions.exp: Cap Classique is South Africa's term for sparkling wine whose second fermentation took place in the bottle in which it is sold, led by Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. The Court adds it at the Certified level to the Introductory examples of Champagne, Crémant, Cava and Franciacorta.

questions.q: Lambrusco, the Court's Certified example of the tank method, is made chiefly in which Italian region?
questions.exp: Lambrusco is the red, often frothy wine of Emilia, around Modena and Reggio, with a smaller zone over the border in Lombardy near Mantua. Most is made by the tank method, which keeps its fresh red fruit, and it comes dry as well as sweet.

questions.q: Besides ancestral method and pétillant naturel, which French name does the Court give the method that finishes the first fermentation in bottle?
questions.exp: The Court lists Ancestral Method, Méthode Rurale and Pétillant Naturel, or pet-nat, as names for one process: the first fermentation is paused part way, the wine is bottled and fermentation finishes inside, with no second fermentation. It is bottled at much lower pressure than Champagne and often left undisgorged.

questions.q: By the Court's figures, a tank method sparkling wine can go from harvest to final bottling in as little as how many days?
questions.exp: In the Charmat or cuve close method the second fermentation runs in a pressurised tank and is complete in four to five days, then the wine is filtered and bottled with no riddling or disgorging. That saving of time and cost is the method's whole case, and the Court calls it the best process for aromatic grape varieties.

questions.q: Which sparkling wine best suits a fresh peach tart, needing to be light, sweeter than the dessert and full of the grape's own aroma?
questions.exp: Moscato d'Asti is made in tank, which keeps Moscato's grapey, floral aroma, and, low in alcohol and rich in sugar, it stays sweeter than a fruit dessert. The three traditional method wines are dry and autolytic, better with salty, fried or rich savoury food than with a sweet tart; the Court asks how the method shapes the pairing.

questions.q: Which of these sparkling wines, made in tank with no riddling or disgorging, is the usual value pour on a by the glass list?
questions.exp: Prosecco takes its second fermentation in a pressurised tank, so it skips months on the lees, riddling and disgorging and costs far less to make than Champagne, Franciacorta or Cap Classique, all traditional method wines. A well built list offers bubbles at several price points, with a tank wine at the base and traditional method wines above it.

questions.q: Hand riddling on a pupitre takes several weeks. About how long does a gyropalette usually need to riddle its cage of bottles?
questions.exp: A gyropalette turns and tilts a whole cage of around five hundred bottles at once under a programme, finishing in a few days to a week what a skilled riddler takes weeks to do by hand. It saves labour and cellar space and gives a consistent result, which is why the Court asks its time, cost and efficacy.
